transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Cora Vekulman.
Alaska's Democratic Senate candidate, Mary Peltola,
is dismissing a New York Times report.
It alleges her campaign was part of efforts to put another Senate candidate on the ballot
with the same name as Alaska's incumbent Republican Senator, Dan Sullivan.
That recruit is retired teacher, Dan J. Sullivan.
Dan J. Sullivan, not the incumbent Republican Senator, denies this.
NPR has not independently confirmed the Times reporting.
President Trump campaigned yesterday in Ohio.
From member station WOSU, George Shilcock reports
Trump attacked Peltola and other Democratic officials.
Trump said the Democrat running for U.S. Senate in Alaska should be investigated,
alleging she helped put a man on the ballot who shares the same name
as Republican U.S. Senator Dan Sullivan to divert votes.
She should be removed from the ballot and prosecuted,
and so should the fake Dan Sullivan.
Trump also attacked Minnesota Congresswoman Ilhan Omar
and Governor Tim Walz.
Trump said he wants Walz and Omar investigated too
and appeared to joke that Walz should face capital punishment.
They'd give him the electric chair.
This guy's going to retire. Nothing happens.
Although, I must say, I understand there are lots of investigations going on.
Trump also criticized Ohio Democrats like former U.S. Senators Sherrod Brown
but didn't make similar comments.
For NPR News, I'm George Shilcock.
Nearly all of the ballots have been counted from Israel's elections this week.
NPR's Daniel Estrin says none of the two main political parties won outright.
Neither side has a clear majority.
The remaining votes that will still be counted are not expected to change that.
The parties, each party would need 61 seats in the parliament to form a majority.
Netanyahu and his allies so far have won 53 seats.
Gadi Eisenkot and his allies have won 48 seats.
So neither has the 61-seat majority that they would need to form a government.
NPR's Daniel Estrin reporting.
Hackers cracked the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's personnel files.
NPR's Vanessa Romo has more.
An activist group called the Department of Peace stole troves of data
by subverting DHS's single sign-on system, according to an online statement.
Now that information, which identifies 21,000 employees with the U.S. Customs and Border Protection
and reveals about 7,000 ICE employees, is available in a searchable database.
Ryan Adignan, one of the activists who helped create it, says publishing the data is a public service.
Employees of the DHS need to be able to be identified
and have their names out there for reasons like sending public records requests.
In a message attached to the database, the hacker said, quote,
"They have our information, so it's only fair that we have theirs."
Vanessa Romo, NPR News.
You're listening to NPR.
The government says the U.S. economy grew 3.4 percent between July and September.
The second quarter growth was stronger than the previous quarter,
but at the same time, Americans are struggling with inflation
and things that are costly are just not affordable.
A separate report today says inflation in September accelerated 3.6 percent from a year ago.
As AI becomes more common in the workplace,
some employees are seeking religious exemptions from using it.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports some legal experts say those requests could create new challenges for employers
and potentially lead to lawsuits.
One of the latest cases comes out of the University of Kentucky,
where a research administrator was granted an exemption from using AI at work,
citing his deeply held humanist beliefs.
Whitney Barth, a professor at Emory Law School, says granting those exemptions
could become more complicated as AI becomes part of everyday work.
An employer has to accommodate religion except if it leads to substantial increase cost in the overall business.
Depending on what those costs look like and depending on the role that AI plays,
it may also, frankly, depend on the role that the individual has within the organization.
Barth says disputes over what qualifies for an exemption from AI could eventually end up in court.
Windsor Johnston, NPR News.
Officials in Spain say that now 69 people were killed in yesterday's collision of two trains.
Authorities are still investigating the crash scene.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola dismisses NYT report on same-name Senate candidate scheme
Trump in Ohio attacks Peltola, Ilhan Omar, and Tim Walz, calling for investigations and prosecution
Israel's election results leave neither Netanyahu's nor Eisenkot's bloc with the 61-seat majority needed
Activist group Department of Peace publishes searchable database of DHS and ICE employee personnel data
U.S. economy grew 3.4 percent in July through September, outpacing the prior quarter
September inflation accelerates to 3.6 percent from a year earlier, according to new report
Employees seek religious exemptions from AI use at work, raising possible employer lawsuits, including University of Kentucky case
Death toll from Spain's two-train collision rises to 69 as investigators examine the crash scene
